                            Parity in Shallow QAC Circuits:
                      Correlation Decay and Exact Lower Bounds
                                                  Shiva Kintali∗

                                               September 5, 2026



                                                     Abstract
              We prove two exponential bounds for single-output parity computation by shallow QAC
          circuits. At entangling depth at most three, uniform-input parity correlation is at most Ke−κn ,
          independently of circuit size and ancillary width. At entangling depth at most four, exact parity
          requires at least ecn multiqubit gates for all sufficiently large n. The constants are absolute.
          The model allows arbitrary one-qubit gates, arbitrary-arity generalized Toffoli gates, any finite
          number of input-independent product-initialized ancillas, including mixed product states, and
          unrestricted final garbage outside one measured qubit.


1        Introduction
Parity asks whether an odd number of input bits are one. Its full dependence on the input makes it a
basic test of how information passes through a shallow circuit. Classical constant-depth circuits with
unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and NOT gates cannot compute parity with polynomial size;
switching lemmas and Fourier concentration explain this limitation [9, 13]. For quantum circuits,
interference and unbounded-arity gates make an ordinary bounded-fan-in light-cone argument
insufficient.
    We study circuits with one computational-basis copy of each input bit, generalized Toffoli gates,
and arbitrary one-qubit unitaries. Depth counts layers of multiqubit gates with pairwise disjoint
supports, including controls; one-qubit gates contribute neither to depth nor to size. Throughout,
depth d means entangling depth at most d. Ancillas start in a fixed product state independent
of the input. The numbers of gates and ancillary wires may be arbitrarily large but finite. Only
one measured output qubit must report the answer: the inputs may be overwritten and all other
outputs may contain garbage. There are no intermediate measurements, postselection, additional
supplied input copies, or free fan-out gates.
    Moore introduced the QAC0 model and related coherent parity, fan-out, and cat-state prepara-
tion [15]; see also [7, 3]. With fan-out gates, constant-depth quantum circuits admit approximate
counting and arithmetic constructions [11] and exact threshold constructions [18]. Here QAC denotes
the gate-set model without a polynomial resource restriction, while QAC0 denotes constant-depth
families with polynomially many wires and gates. The distinction matters: one of our conclusions
rules out fixed parity advantage at depth three regardless of finite circuit size, whereas the other
gives an exponential gate requirement at depth four.
    ∗
        Email: shiva.kintali@gmail.com      Homepage: shivakintali.github.io.




                                                         1
1.1   Two main results
Let χ(x) = (−1)x1 +···+xn for x ∈ {0, 1}n , n ≥ 1. A fixed binary measurement on the designated
output qubit has effects E+ , E− ≥ 0 with E+ + E− = I. Label its outcomes +1 for even parity and
−1 for odd parity, and set Ao = E+ − E− . For a circuit C with full output state ρx , define

                                  c(C, Ao ) = Ex∈{0,1}n χ(x) Tr(ρx Ao ).

Here the average is uniform and Ao is tensored with the identity on all other wires. Since −I ≤ Ao ≤ I,
it is a Hermitian contraction. The correct-outcome probability on input x is [1 + χ(x) Tr(ρx Ao )]/2,
so the uniform-input success probability is (1 + c(C, Ao ))/2. Our main results are:
   (i) Exponential correlation decay at depth three. There are absolute K0 ≥ 1 and κ > 0 such that

                                            |c(C, Ao )| ≤ 6K0 e−κn

       for every depth-three circuit, independently of gate count, ancillary width, and gate arity
       (Theorem 1). Thus no fixed positive uniform-input advantage, and hence no fixed worst-case
       advantage, is possible for sufficiently large n. A zero-ancilla construction has correlation
       exp(−Θ(n)), showing that the exponential order is attainable (Proposition 14); this does not
       assert a matching constant in the exponent or a fixed worst-case advantage.
  (ii) Exponential gate growth for exact depth four. There are absolute c∗ > 0 and n0 such that
       every exact depth-four parity circuit on n ≥ n0 inputs has at least ec∗ n multiqubit gates
       (Theorem 2). The ancillary width and gate arities remain unrestricted and finite.
Both statements permit general binary measurements on any designated qubit, including an input
wire, and arbitrary final garbage. They also hold for mixed product ancillary states. They do not
allow arbitrary entangled initial advice, and they do not resolve parity at every constant depth. The
depth-four theorem concerns exact computation; it does not exclude all bounded-error depth-four
families.
    Explicit constants for the principal bounds are recorded in Appendix A.

1.2   A common estimate and two circuit applications
For the proof overview, take pure product initialization; the mixed-product case follows by Lemma 3.
A one-input source is a first-layer gate component, or an untouched input singleton, containing
exactly one variable input. All its other wires start in fixed pure product states. Its ports are its
nonempty intersections with second-layer gates, together with one additional port of idle wires
if any remain. Let ρ0 , ρ1 be the source states after the first layer. Writing F = (ρ0 − ρ1 )/2 and
ρ̄ = (ρ0 + ρ1 )/2, we assign weight hj = 1 − λmax (ρ̄j ) to port j, where ρ̄j is the reduced average state
on that port. Lemma 4 gives the budget j hj ≤ 1/2 + 2/e, independently of physical width.
                                            P

    For r independent one-input sources, Theorem 11 bounds the absolute full-parity coefficient of
any port-product effect E = j Ej , 0 ≤ Ej ≤ Ij , after the second layer by K0 e−ar , for absolute
                                N

constants K0 ≥ 1 and a > 0. An input-independent resource operator of arbitrary finite dimension
and trace norm at most one may be tensored with the sources; its ports are included in the product
defining E. In expansion branches this operator can be non-Hermitian, so the resulting functional
is interpreted as a possibly complex trace pairing. Each effect Ej may act jointly on all physical
qubits of its port. This generality is needed for the depth-four certificate.
    The proof calls a second-layer gate heavy when the sum of the source weights incident to it
exceeds a fixed threshold. Heavy gates are treated by an exact reflection expansion. Several
corrections can touch different ports of one source; they must be treated as one joint insertion. A
centered rank-one inequality transfers the source’s upper bound on the squared trace norm of F

                                                    2
after random port retention to this insertion, using the original weights. The remaining light gates
and private ports receive independent random choices; sources meeting the same light gate share its
choice. Bounded differences controls the resulting dependence between sources. A convex estimate
for the loss from a joint insertion controls terms with many heavy-gate corrections. Summing
separately over terms with few and many corrections gives exponential decay.
    Two arguments then connect this estimate to parity. For depth three, a rank-two correction
handles the signed state of a first-layer gate containing many input bits. Combining this expansion
with conditioning on the smaller components gives an exponential bound for events that factor
over individual physical qubits, with arbitrary first layers (Theorem 12). Pulling back one output
observable through the third layer expresses it as a linear combination of such events with total
absolute coefficient mass at most six (Lemma 13) and proves the correlation theorem.
    For exact depth four, the cleanup in Lemma 15 uses classical and quantum restrictions to retain
r ≥ n/3 variable inputs with one variable per source, without increasing depth or gate count. Output
determinism yields a certificate involving the sector on which the final output gate acts as the identity.
Label each control by its input source or the grouped input-free resource, and by its gate-or-idle
incidence in layers two and three. The resulting cells number at most (r + 1)(m2 + 1)(m3 + 1),
where m2 , m3 count gates in those two layers (Lemma 18). Each cell lies in one two-layer port, so
its effect may be treated jointly within that port. The number of cells is polynomial in the retained
input count and gate count and is independent of ancillary width. Applying the common event
bound to these cells forces exponentially many gates. Exactness is used in the depth-four argument.

1.3   Related work and attribution
Ancilla-restricted lower bounds at general depths. Fang, Fenner, Green, Homer, and
Zhang [5] proved logarithmic depth lower bounds for clean exact implementations of coherent parity
and fan-out with constantly many ancillas, together with a depth–ancilla tradeoff. Here clean means
that the ancillary registers are returned to their initial zero state. Their convention counts one-qubit
gates in the depth; the logarithmic conclusion is unchanged by the constant-factor conversion to
our convention. Bera [2] gave a different lower-bound method excluding ancilla-free constant-depth
exact parity circuits.
    Nadimpalli, Parham, Vasconcelos, and Yuen [16] developed Pauli-spectrum concentration, in the
spirit of the classical Fourier-analytic approach. For polynomial-size circuits of fixed depth d, their
                                                                           1/d
Theorem 33 implies uniform-input parity success at most 1/2 + 2−Ω(n ) when the ancilla count is
a sufficiently small constant multiple of n1/d . Anshu, Dong, Ou, and Yao [1] used spectral-norm
approximation by low-degree operators to obtain the stated ancilla threshold Ω(n    e 1+3−d ) for parity.
Dong, Ou, and Yao [4] improved the corresponding parity threshold to Ω(n       e 1+2−d ) using operator
and unitary dilation; in the small-ancilla regime of their Corollary 3.3, uniform-input success is
at most 1/2 + O(d/n). The tilde suppresses logarithmic factors in these resource thresholds. At
depth four, the two stated superlinear thresholds have exponents 82/81 and 17/16. These three
spectral methods apply across arbitrary constant depths and allow arbitrary input-independent
ancillary states. Our removal of any ancilla-count restriction must instead be read together with
the product-initialization assumption.
    The quoted exponents are the papers’ simplified corollary thresholds, not optimal inversions
of their estimates. At fixed depth d ≥ 1, the cited estimates give a polynomial that uniformly
approximates the single-output acceptance probability and has degree O(N       e 1−α ), where N is the
                                    −d     −d
total number of wires and α = 3 or 2 , respectively. For any fixed positive success advantage,
                                                e 1/(1−α) ); see [1, Theorem 4.1] and [4, Theorem 3.1].
they therefore imply an ancillary requirement Ω(n
Indeed, let p(x) be the probability of outputting 1 (odd parity). Since Ex χ(x) = 0, uniform-input

                                                    3
success at least 1/2 + δ gives Ex χ(x)p(x) ≤ −δ. Every polynomial of total degree less than n is
orthogonal to χ on the uniform Boolean cube: each of its monomials omits some variable, and
averaging over that variable cancels its contribution. Thus, for any such polynomial pe,
                               δ ≤ Ex χ(x)(p(x) − pe(x)) ≤ kp − pek∞ ,
where the norm is the maximum over {0, 1}n . Consequently, a uniform approximation with error
less than δ requires degree at least n. The parameter restriction in [4, Theorem 3.1] permits the
required choice of its accuracy parameter of order log N at fixed depth and initial operator degree
one, for sufficiently large N . The approximation error in [1, Theorem 4.1] also tends to zero at fixed
depth. Inverting n ≤ e    O(N 1−α ) yields N ≥ e
                                               Ω(n1/(1−α) ). Since 1/(1 − α) > 1, subtracting the n
input wires preserves this asymptotic lower bound on the ancillary count. Thus the directly derived
depth-four exponents are 81/80 and 16/15, respectively.

Fixed-depth lower bounds and approximate constructions. Rosenthal [17, Corollary 1.6
and Theorem 1.7] studied the coherent parity operation, which adds parity into a target and
preserves the other input wires, allowing final garbage. He obtained an Ω(n/(d + 1)) multiqubit-gate
requirement for worst-case coherent approximation with squared-overlap fidelity exceeding 1/2 by
a fixed positive amount. At depth two, fidelity on a specified product quantum input is at most
1/2 + exp(−Ω(n)), independently of size. These are coherent fidelity statements, not average-case
Boolean-success bounds; allowing garbage does not remove input preservation.
     His Corollary 1.2 also gives, for every d ≥ 7 and 0 < ε < 1, circuits of size and ancilla count
exp(poly(n1/d ) log(n/ε)) whose output has squared Euclidean distance at most ε from the ideal
coherent parity output tensored with an all-zero ancillary register, on every pure quantum input.
This phase-sensitive state-vector guarantee permits a small deviation of the actual ancillas from zero.
Such greater-depth approximate constructions are consistent with an exact depth-four lower bound.
     Fenner, Grier, Padé, and Thierauf [6] proved that exact single-output parity on more than
three non-target input bits is impossible at depth two, regardless of gate count or the number of
product-initialized ancillas. Their proof uses irreducible polynomials and entanglement. Joshi, Tal,
Vasconcelos, and Wright [12] proved exact depth-three impossibility for n > 100, again independently
of size and the number of product-initialized ancillas, and a depth-two single-output parity-correlation
                 √
bound exp(−Ω( n)). Their exact analysis uses quantum restrictions and classical AC0 simulation.
     Gretta, Gupta, and Joshi [8, Theorems 1.1 and 1.3] relate parity lower bounds to Fourier
concentration and show that inverse-polynomial average-case parity correlation suffices for exact
parity computation under QAC0 reductions. These results concern constant-depth classes with a
change in depth; they do not preserve the specific depth-four restriction studied here.
     For exact parity with unrestricted product ancillary width, Theorem 2 reaches depth four with
an exponential gate lower bound. The depth-three result of [12] excludes circuits of every size at
that smaller depth. Compared with general-depth ancilla bounds, it removes any numerical limit on
product-initialized ancillary space at this fixed depth. Compared with Rosenthal’s general-depth gate
bound, it gives an exponential lower bound for exact computation and applies to the more permissive
single-output task. It neither excludes exponentially large depth-four circuits nor establishes a lower
bound at every constant depth.
     Theorem 1 supplies a different improvement: it bounds average-case parity correlation at depth
three by exp(−Ω(n)) without a size or product-ancilla-width restriction. The exact depth-three
obstruction and the depth-two correlation result cited above do not themselves give this conclusion.

Inherited ingredients. Product-reflection normalization is used in [17]. Our exact cleanup
reproduces the mechanism of [12, Lemma 4.1], including the preparation of the fixed-parity pairs and

                                                   4
gate accounting. The final-gate active/identity-sector decomposition appears in [12, Section 2.3.1].
The additional depth-four step is the quantitative certificate and its grouping into control cells.
Bounded differences and the bounded-range exponential-moment inequality are classical tools [14, 10].
We also use standard trace-norm duality, Schatten Hölder, convexity, and spectral decomposition.
The contributions are the source and joint-insertion estimates, their network summation, and the
circuit interfaces; no historical priority claim is made for general matrix or concentration inequalities.

Organization. Section 2 fixes the model and states the main theorems. Sections 3 and 4 prove
the shared source and event estimates. Section 5 proves the depth-three theorem and gives the
matching exponential-order construction. Section 6 proves the exact depth-four theorem. The
appendices give explicit constants and a self-contained proof of the concentration inequality used in
the main argument.


2    Circuit model, notation, and statements
Registers, gates, and resources. Fix integers N ≥ n ≥ 1. A circuit acts on N qubits, with one
copy of the classical input |xi, x ∈ {0, 1}n , and a pure ancillary state

requires only one-qubit unitaries.
    A generalized controlled-Z gate on a set S of at least two qubits is

For any target t ∈ S, conjugating this gate by the Hadamard on t gives the generalized Toffoli with
controls S \ {t}:                                        ^

 Here z ∈ {0, 1}S\{t} labels the control register and b ∈ {0, 1} labels the target; their displayed order
 is only a notation for the tensor factors. The same conjugation gives the reverse conversion. Thus
 these two gate sets are equivalent once one-qubit unitaries are free, as in the depth convention
 below.
     For an integer d ≥ 0, a circuit has entangling depth at most d if it can be written with d layers
 of controlled-Z gates, some possibly empty, with pairwise disjoint gate supports within each layer,
 including all control and target wires. Arbitrary products of one-qubit unitaries may occur before,
 between, and after these layers; they contribute neither to entangling depth nor to size. We use
“depth d” to mean entangling depth at most d. The size M is the total number of multiqubit gates.
 Every circuit has finitely many wires and gates, but we impose no a priori bound on N or on
 gate arities as functions of n. There is one designated output qubit o, which may be an original
 input wire. Every other wire may contain arbitrary final garbage; input preservation and ancillary
 uncomputation are not required.

Parity coefficients, events, and norms. All logarithms are natural unless explicitly stated
otherwise. Write [k] = {1, . . . , k} for integers k ≥ 0, with [0] = ∅, and put χ(x) = (−1)x1 +···+xn .

circuit stage, write hBix = Tr(ρx B). In such expectations, an operator specified on only some wires
is tensored with identity on the remaining wires.

Output conventions and the main theorems. Let ρx = Cρin                 ∗
                                                                    x C be the full output state. For
pure initialization, write |Ψx i = C(|xi ⊗ |αi), so that ρx = |Ψx ihΨx |. A binary measurement on o
consists of effects E+ , E− ≥ 0 with E+ + E− = Io . Label its outcomes +1 for even parity and −1
for odd parity, and put
                                     Ao = E+ − E− = 2E+ − Io .
Thus Ao is a one-qubit Hermitian contraction and Tr(ρx Ao ) is the mean of the signed measurement
outcome. Conversely, every one-qubit Hermitian contraction defines such a measurement by
E± = (Io ± Ao )/2. For a general binary measurement the outcomes are these labels, not necessarily
the eigenvalues of Ao .
   We say that C, with its specified measurement Ao , computes parity exactly if

                             Tr(ρx Ao ) = χ(x)       for every x ∈ {0, 1}n .                         (2)

Because n ≥ 1, both parity values occur. Since Tr(ρx Ao ) is a convex combination of the eigenvalues
of Ao , weighted by the reduced state on o, attaining each of the extreme expectations +1 and −1
forces both values to occur in the spectrum of Ao . Since o is a qubit, Ao is therefore a Hermitian
unitary with one eigenvalue of each sign. Its measurement effects are consequently the rank-one
spectral projectors E± = (Io ±Ao )/2. A one-qubit change of basis turns this into computational-basis
measurement, so allowing general binary measurements does not enlarge the exact computation
model. This argument also applies to mixed output states.
    For pure initialization in the exact case, let |a± i be fixed unit eigenvectors of Ao . For y = χ(x),
the projector Py = Io +yA

                             ⊗ Irest satisfies

For this Hermitian unitary Ao , exactness is consequently equivalent to

                                    |Ψx i = |aχ(x) i ∗ o ⊗ |γx i ∗ rest

for a unit vector γx that may depend arbitrarily on x. The purity used here follows from pure
initialization and unitary evolution. No preservation of the other registers is asserted.
    For a general binary measurement, define the uniform-input parity correlation by

                                     c(C, Ao ) = Ex χ(x) Tr(ρx Ao ).                                 (3)

This is real and belongs to [−1, 1], since ρx is a density operator and Ao is a Hermitian contraction.
On input x, the probability of the correct outcome is [1 + χ(x) Tr(ρx Ao )]/2. Hence the average
success probability is exactly
                                                       1 + c(C, Ao )
                                      psucc (C, Ao ) =               .
                                                             2
Because every input has positive uniform probability, average success one is equivalent to success
on every input. Thus c(C, Ao ) = 1 if and only if C with measurement Ao computes parity exactly.
In particular, uniform-input success at least 1/2 + ε implies c(C, Ao ) ≥ 2ε. A worst-case success
guarantee implies the same uniform-input guarantee, but the converse is not assumed.

Theorem 1 (Exponential correlation at depth three). There are absolute constants K0 ≥ 1 and
κ > 0 such that every circuit in the model above of entangling depth at most three satisfies
                                                                         1
                      |c(C, Ao )| ≤ 6K0 e−κn ,        psucc (C, Ao ) ≤     + 3K0 e−κn .
                                                                         2
The constants are independent of the finite gate count, ancillary width, gate arities, product ancillary
state, and binary one-qubit measurement. The same statement holds for mixed product ancillary
states. In particular, one may use
                                                                     −27 n
                                  |c(C, Ao )| ≤ min{1, 1800e−2               }.

   The qualitative bound is proved in Section 5; Appendix A derives the displayed numerical
specialization.

Theorem 2 (Exact depth-four lower bound). There exist an absolute constant c∗ > 0 and an
absolute integer n0 ≥ 1 such that, for every n ≥ n0 and every circuit in the model above of entangling
depth at most four that computes n-bit parity exactly, its multiqubit-gate count satisfies

                                                 M ≥ e c∗ n .

The constants are independent of the finite number of product-initialized ancillary wires, their initial
state, all gate arities, and the binary one-qubit measurement. The same assertion holds for mixed
product ancillary states by Lemma 3. In particular, exact parity has no polynomial-size depth-four
QAC circuit family, even when only multiqubit gates are counted.

    The proof is completed in Section 6, using the exponential event estimate and parity-preserving
cleanup from Sections 4 and 6.1. It permits arbitrary garbage and also covers an output qubit that
is an original input wire.

Lemma 3 (Mixed product initialization). For a fixed circuit and measurement, any bound on
|c(C, Ao )| uniform over pure product ancillary states extends to input-independent mixed product
ancillary states. The same holds for the absolute full-parity coefficient of any fixed output operator,
including a non-Hermitian operator. If a fixed circuit and measurement compute parity exactly with
mixed product ancillas, they do so with a pure product ancillary state on the same wires. Thus the
exact lower bound also extends without changing depth, gate count, or arity.

Proof. Expand each τq in an orthonormal eigenbasis. Their tensor product is a finite convex
combination τ = z pz |αz ihαz | of pure product states, where pz ≥ 0, z pz = 1, and the weights
                   P                                                      P
                                             P
are independent of x. Consequently ρx = z pz ρx,z , where ρx,z is the output state for ancillary
input |αz i. Linearity gives c(C, Ao ) = z pz cz (C, Ao ), so the triangle inequality proves the first
                                         P

claim; the same calculation applies to any fixed signed trace pairing.
    For the exact assertion, let sz (x) ∈ [0, 1] be the correct-output probability for input x and
ancillary state |αz i. Exactness of the mixture implies, for every x,
                                        X                  X
                               0=1−          pz sz (x) =        pz (1 − sz (x)).
                                         z                 z

Every term is nonnegative. Thus, for every fixed z with pz > 0, we have sz (x) = 1 for every input x.
At least one such z exists, and choosing it once gives a single pure product ancillary state that works
for all inputs. The circuit, measurement, and physical wires are unchanged. The argument includes
an absent ancillary register, whose decomposition has one scalar component of weight one.

                                                      8
3    A local source lemma
For each fixed classical input, pure product initialization and disjointness imply that the state after
the first multiqubit layer is a tensor product over gate components: the gate supports and untouched
singleton wires. A source in this section is one such component with exactly one variable input and
any finite number of fixed pure product ancillas. Denote its variable-input wire by d. Partition the
source wires into nonempty ports, indexed by J = {0, 1, . . . , m} for an integer m ≥ 0. The owner
port 0 contains d; all other ports contain only ancillary wires. This partition is arbitrary and will
later be chosen from second-layer incidences. For A ⊆ J , the notation TrAc means tracing all wires
in ports indexed by J \ A. In particular, if A contains only ancillary-port indices, its complement
includes the owner.
    Using the reflection normal form and a local change of basis on d, write the source gate as
                                                                       O
                         G = I − 2|1ih1|d ⊗ Πanc ,         Πanc =             |vq ihvq |,
                                                                      q∈Anc

where Anc is the set of ancillary wires in the source. All vectors vq and αq below are unit vectors.
The two possible data inputs u0 , u1 form an orthonormal basis: they are the images of the two
actual data states under the one-qubit basis change that sends the gate’s trigger vector on d to |1i.
                           N
The ancillary input is α = q∈Anc αq . One-qubit unitaries after G act within ports; they conjugate
each port marginal and each retained marginal of F , preserving eigenvalues and trace norms. In the
insertion lemma below they can also be absorbed into the inserted operator without changing its
rank or norm, so we omit them here.
    An untouched singleton is covered by taking no ancillas and using the formal one-qubit reflection
G = Zd . If its actual output vectors are ϕ0 , ϕ1 , set ux = Zd ϕx , so Gux = ϕx . This is an
analytic representation, not an added multiqubit gate. Empty tensor products are scalars on a
one-dimensional space.

The change is nonnegative; the first inequality uses ξ 2 ≤ 1 and Θ/(ΘA pj ) ≤ 1, the latter being the

Each single-port addition is nonnegative: for ancillary ports this was just proved, and adding the
owner sets f to one. Thus f is nondecreasing under inclusion, completing (ii).

    The partition into ports was arbitrary, so the lemma also applies after merging ports. The port
containing d is designated the owner, and the mixedness of each merged port is computed from its
joint marginal.
Remark 5. The constant 3/4 in (ii) is sharp for majorants of the true squared retained norm. Take
ux = |xi and one ancilla in |0i, apply CNOT from the input to the ancilla, and place the two wires
in separate ports. This is directly a permitted source reflection:

                                                                            |0i − |1i
                        CNOT = I − 2|1ih1|d ⊗ |−ih−|,               |−i =      √      .
                                                                                 2
It has ξ = 1, p0 = 1, and p1 = 1/2, and its signed output is

                                             |00ih00| − |11ih11|
                                       F =                       .
                                                      2
For A = ∅, {0}, {1}, {0, 1}, respectively, the squared retained trace norms are 0, 1, 1, 1. The majorant
above has these same values, so its mean is exactly 3/4. Indeed, any majorant of the true squared
retained norm must have mean at least 3/4 in this example.
    The example also shows why separate insertion penalties cannot be multiplied. Here λ0 = λ1 =
1/2, but
                                                             1
                                 |Tr[(|0ih0| ⊗ |0ih0|)F ]| = > λ0 λ1 .
                                                             2
The joint marginal, rather than a product of single-port bounds, is needed for simultaneous insertions.


                                                   12
Lemma 6 (Rank-one insertion). For a one-input source and any operator T of rank at most one
on port j, put K = Trj [(T ⊗ I)F ]. Then

                                           kKk1 ≤ kT k∞ λj .

In particular, a rank-one contraction gives kKk1 ≤ λj . For a union J ⊆ J of ports, take T of rank
at most one on that union and put K = TrJ [(T ⊗ I)F ]; TrJ traces all wires in the ports indexed by
J. The same statement holds with the joint marginal ρ̄J = TrJ c ρ̄ and λJ = λmax (ρ̄J ).
    If Y1 , Y2 , Y3 are contractions on the remaining wires, then kY1 KY2 k1 ≤ kT k∞ λj and | Tr(Y3 K)| ≤
kT k∞ λj . Further partial traces cannot increase the trace-norm bound. For insertion on a union J,
these consequences hold with λJ in place of λj . All these assertions concern unnormalized operators.

Proof. Define the isometry W : C2 → Hsource by W |xi = ψx . Let Z = |0ih0| − |1ih1| on its logical
input. Then
                               F = W ZW ∗ /2,     ρ̄ = W W ∗ /2.
For a unit vector u on the inserted port define Wu = (hu| ⊗ I)W . Cyclicity of trace gives

                         kWu k22 = Tr[(|uihu| ⊗ I)W W ∗ ] = 2hu|ρ̄j |ui ≤ 2λj .

For T = |uihv| with u, v unit, direct partial tracing gives

                                           K = Wv ZWu∗ /2.

Schatten Hölder and kWv Zk2 = kWv k2 yield
                                          1
                                    kKk1 ≤ kWv k2 kWu k2 ≤ λj .
                                          2
Every nonzero rank-one T has the form s|uihv| with s = kT k∞ and u, v unit; scaling proves the
stated bound. For T = 0 it is immediate. Nothing requires T or K to be Hermitian.
    The same calculation treats a union of ports as one tensor factor. It includes J = ∅, when the
inserted register is scalar and λJ = Tr ρ̄ = 1, and J = J , when the remaining register is scalar
and λJ = 1/2. The remaining-wire assertions follow from kY1 KY2 k1 ≤ kY1 k∞ kKk1 kY2 k∞ and
trace-norm duality. For completeness, partial-trace contractivity also holds without Hermiticity:

                            kTrB Xk1 =     sup | Tr[(IB ⊗ Y )X]| ≤ kXk1 .
                                         kY k∞ ≤1

Here Y acts on the untraced register, and kIB ⊗ Y k∞ = kY k∞ , so no dimension factor occurs. The
insertion argument uses only that W is an isometry. The special mixedness values and budget
proved above still require the one-reflection, product-initialized source structure.


4     Exponential event bounds from the shared source estimate
4.1    Ports, joint resources, and random activation
Take r independent one-input sources and a fixed, input-independent resource operator σ with
kσk1 ≤ 1, in tensor product with the sources. Group all resource wires before defining ports. For
each group, its ports are its nonempty intersections with second-layer gate supports and, if nonempty,
its remaining idle wires. Let E be a fixed tensor product of positive contractions over these ports.
A factor may be entangled within one port. One-qubit gates before and after the second layer can

                                                    13
be absorbed into source states and event factors, respectively; they act within ports and preserve
the source weights and norms. The signed input to the second layer is
                                              r
                                              O
                              Σ=σ⊗                  Fi ,             Fi = (ρi,0 − ρi,1 )/2.
                                              i=1

The resource is not assumed to factor over its ports and need not be Hermitian. For operators X
on B ⊗ A and T on B, trace-norm duality gives

                                      kTrB [(T ⊗ I)X]k1 ≤ kT k∞ kXk1 .                                              (8)

Indeed, pair the partial trace with an operator Y of norm at most one; then | Tr[(T ⊗ Y )X]| ≤
kT k∞ kXk1 . This includes ordinary partial-trace contractivity and requires no Hermiticity of X.
    Represent each second-layer gate by a real vertex and each idle port by a private vertex. Every
wire belongs to exactly one vertex and each source has at most one port at that vertex. Write i ∼ g
when source i has a port at gate g. Write the effect and gate at a real vertex as
                                  O                                                                 O
                  Pg = Pres,g ⊗           Pig ,     Dg = I − 2Πg ,               Πg = Πres,g ⊗             Πig ,
                                  i:i∼g                                                            i:i∼g

omitting absent factors. Each present Π factor is a rank-one orthogonal projector; each P factor is
a positive contraction. The pulled-back event is the tensor product of Dg Pg Dg over real vertices
and the idle effects. The exact identity

                            Dg Pg Dg = Pg − 2Πg Pg − 2Pg Πg + 4Πg Pg Πg                                             (9)

has correction coefficient mass eight. Each coefficient-free correction factors into rank-at-most-one
contractions on all its incident ports.

Lemma 7 (Joint random activation). Let a tensor-product operator consist of arbitrary operators
K1 , . . . , Kr on disjoint source groups and an independent resource operator σ with kσk1 ≤ 1. None
of these operators need be Hermitian. Partition its wires into vertices so that each vertex meets each
source in either one whole port or no wires. For any tensor product of positive contractions Eg over
vertices,                        "                   #
                               O                    O                           Y
                          Tr (        Eg )(σ ⊗                Ki )     ≤ EA          kTrVi \A Ki k1 ,              (10)
                                  g                   i                          i

where each vertex belongs to A independently with probability 1/2 and Vi is the vertex set incident
to source i. The partial trace removes the ports of source i at vertices outside A. Empty registers
and products have the scalar conventions of Section 2.

Proof. Put Γg = 2Eg − Ig . It is a Hermitian contraction, and
                                                                                        
                                   O                           O                O
                                          Eg = EA (                 Γg ) ⊗ (         Ig ) .
                                      g                       g∈A                ∈A
                                                                                g/

For fixed A, trace the inactive wires in each source and in the joint resource. The resource marginal
has trace norm at most one by (8). The active operator has norm at most one. Trace-norm duality
and multiplicativity on tensor products give the asserted product bound, and averaging proves the
claim. Different sources may share a coin; no expectation is factored over sources, and no tensor
factorization of the resource’s ports is used.

4.2    Retention after a joint insertion
Lemma 8 (Rank-one contraction bound). Let ρ0 , ρ1 be any density operators on B ⊗ A, and put
F = (ρ0 − ρ1 )/2. For a rank-at-most-one contraction T on B, put

                             d = kTrB F k1 ,      ν = kTrB [(T ⊗ I)F ]k1 .

Then
                                      1+d             1 1
                                   ν≤      ,    ν 2 ≤ + d2 .                                     (11)
                                       2              2 2
The operator T and the contracted output need not be Hermitian.
Proof. We prove a stronger centered inequality for every Hermitian F . Write K = TrB [(T ⊗ I)F ],
FA = TrB F , t = kT k∞ , and τ = Tr T . Then

                                      k2K − τ FA k1 ≤ t kF k1 .                                  (12)

The case T = 0 is immediate. Otherwise factor T = |uihv|, so kukkvk = t. For a unit vector z on B,
put Pz = |zihz| and Tzz = hz|T |zi. Cauchy–Schwarz, applied to each term and then to the sum,
gives
                  |Tzz | + |Tzz − τ | ≤ kPz ukkPz vk + k(I − Pz )ukk(I − Pz )vk ≤ t.
Thus Tc = 2T − τ I satisfies |hz|Tc |zi| ≤ t for every unit z. Consequently −tI ≤ Re(eiθ Tc ) ≤ tI for
every real θ, by evaluating its quadratic form on unit vectors. For any unitary U on A, diagonalizing
U shows that Re(Tc ⊗ U ) is a direct sum of blocks Re(eiθ Tc ), each of operator norm at most t. Here
Re X = (X + X ∗ )/2. For Hermitian F , Re Tr(XF ) = Tr[(Re X)F ]. Trace-norm duality therefore
gives
                         k2K − τ FA k1 = max Re Tr[(Tc ⊗ U )F ] ≤ t kF k1 .
                                          U unitary

No Hermiticity of K or T is used. Since kF k1 ≤ 1 and |τ | ≤ t ≤ 1, the triangle inequality yields
2ν ≤ 1 + d. Finally, for 0 ≤ d ≤ 1,
                                          (1 − d)(3 + d)  1
                               1 − ν2 ≥                  ≥ (1 − d2 ).
                                                4         2
This proves (11).

Lemma 9 (Transfer of the original retention majorant). For one source, insert a rank-at-most-
one contraction T on a union B of its original ports. Put K = TrB [(T ⊗ I)F ] and let f0 be the
nondecreasing majorant from Lemma 4. For any subset A of the remaining ports, define

                                fB (A) = min{kKk21 , (1 + f0 (A))/2}.

This majorizes the squared retained norm of K, is at most one, has mean at most 7/8 under
independent fair retention, and has oscillation at most 2hj when a remaining port j is toggled. The
weights are the original source weights, including when the owner or every port is inserted.
Proof. Equation (8) gives kKk1 ≤ 1. Write KA and FA for the respective marginals on A. Trace all
other remaining ports of both density operators defining F before applying Lemma 8 to the inserted
union and A. This gives kKA k21 ≤ (1 + kFA k21 )/2 ≤ (1 + f0 (A))/2. Partial-trace contractivity also
bounds it by kKk21 . Couple fair choices on the remaining ports with independent fair choices AB on
the inserted ports. Monotonicity gives

                                EA f0 (A) ≤ EA,AB f0 (A ∪ AB ) ≤ 3/4.

                                                      15
Hence the new mean is at most 7/8. Halving the original oscillation bound gives 2hj ; clipping at
the fixed number kKk21 cannot increase oscillations. Empty registers are scalar spaces, so the same
argument includes empty inserted or remaining sets and zero insertions. No inserted operator is
renormalized.

Proof. Write W = W (B) and h∪ = h∪ (B). The empty union and W = 0 are immediate. If
B contains the owner, then h∪ = 1/2 and W ≤ Cs < 5/4. Since 4/W > 16/5 > e, we have
Φ(W ) < W/4 < 5/16 < 1/2.
    Suppose B is ancillary-only. Let Θ be the full ancillary trigger probability and pB its probability
on B. Since W > 0, the case Θ = 0 is excluded: all ancillary-only weights would vanish. Also pB = 1
would make every selected port weight zero. Thus 0 < Θ ≤ pB < 1 before any logarithm or division
below is taken. Summing (6) over j ∈ B gives W ≤ 2Θ j∈B (1 − pj ) ≤ 2Θ log(1/pB ); applying (6)

4.4    The exponential source-event theorem
Theorem 11 (Exponential two-layer source bound). There are absolute constants K0 ≥ 1 and
a > 0 with the following property. Let r ≥ 0 be an integer. Consider r independent one-input
first-layer sources as in Section 3 and a tensor-independent resource operator σ with kσk1 ≤ 1,
independent of the input x. Apply a second layer of pairwise wire-disjoint generalized controlled-Z
gates, with arbitrary one-qubit gates before and after it. Use the nonempty source-by-second-gate
ports and private idle ports defined above, including ports on the resource.
    Let E be a fixed tensor product of positive contractions over these ports. After absorbing the
adjacent one-qubit gates as above, set
                                                      r
                                      "                             !         #
                                                                        U2∗
                                                      O
                            q(x) = Tr EU2 σ ⊗               ρi,xi                 ,       x ∈ {0, 1}r ,
                                                      i=1

where ρi,xi is the state of input source i and U2 is the second multiqubit layer. All gates and effects
are independent of x. The full signed coefficient of q satisfies

                                                  |qb([r])| ≤ K0 e−ar .

The functional q(x) is an event probability if σ is a density operator, and may be complex otherwise.
The bound is independent of gate count, port widths, and finite resource dimension. For r = 0 the
coefficient is the single trace pairing, of magnitude at most one. An absent resource is the scalar 1.
Proof. The r = 0 assertion follows from trace-norm duality. Assume r ≥ 1. Linearity of uniform
signed averaging gives Σ = σ ⊗ ri=1 Fi and qb([r]) = Tr(U2∗ EU2 Σ). Use the original port weights
                                N

hig , with g hig ≤ Cs and hig = 0 for absent ports. All rows refer only to input sources, not the
          P

exceeds w. Let H be the set of heavy gates and NH = |H|. The row budgets imply

                                                    NH ≤ Cs r/w.                                                  (14)

Expand all heavy gates. For every g ∈ H, expand its pulled-back event exactly:

                               Dg Pg Dg = Pg − 2Πg Pg − 2Pg Πg + 4Πg Pg Πg .

After removing the scalar coefficients −2, −2, 4, the three correction operators factor over source
ports into contractions of rank at most one, as in (9). A zero correction can be omitted. The base
term Pg is a product of positive port effects and is split into private vertices.
    Choose a correction set S ⊆ H and, for each g ∈ S, a type `g ∈ {1, 2, 3}. Denote its coefficient-free

                      (`)

5     Depth-three correlation and its exponential order
5.1    Removing the first-layer input-arity restriction
The source theorem assumes one variable per input component. We now remove that assumption
by expanding large first-layer components before applying the theorem. The event must factor over
physical qubits at this interface, because the expansion changes the source partition.
Theorem 12 (Arbitrary first-layer inputs). With K0 as in Theorem 11, there is an absolute κ > 0
with the following property. Let C (2) = L2 D2 L1 D1 L0 be the two-layer prefix of a circuit in the

5.2   One measured output
Lemma 13 (One-output pullback). Conjugating a one-qubit Hermitian contraction by a disjoint
layer of product reflections expresses it as a linear combination of positive physical-qubit product
events with total absolute coefficient mass at most six. Local unitaries before or after the layer
preserve this claim.

Proof. Absorb the output’s final local unitary into Ao . Gates disjoint from o cancel, leaving at most
one gate. If it is present, write
                                                              O
             D = (I − P ) ⊗ Io + P ⊗ Ro ,          P =              |vj ihvj |,     Ro = Io − 2|vo ihvo |.
                                                          j∈S\{o}

Since P (I − P ) = 0, direct multiplication gives

                  D(I ⊗ Ao )D = I ⊗ Ao − 2P ⊗ Bo ,                   Bo = (Ao − Ro Ao Ro )/2.                (19)

Both Ao and Bo are Hermitian, and kBo k∞ ≤ (kAo k∞ + kRo Ao Ro k∞ )/2 ≤ 1. Their spectral
decompositions into two rank-one qubit projectors have coefficient absolute sums at most two each,

                                                          21
yielding total mass at most 2 + 2 · 2 = 6. Every resulting factor is identity or a rank-one qubit
projector, with identity on wires outside the gate. Degenerate eigenspaces may be resolved in any
orthonormal basis. If no gate meets o, only the first spectral decomposition is needed. Finally,
conjugation by a local layer preserves the physical-product form and positivity.

Proof of Theorem 1. Pad with empty layers if necessary. Pull the output observable through the
final local layer and then the third multiqubit layer by Lemma 13. For C = L3 D3 L2 D2 L1 D1 L0 ,
the remaining prefix is C (2) = L2 D2 L1 D1 L0 . Each resulting physical-product event has full-
parity coefficient of absolute value at most K0 e−κn by Theorem 12. The triangle inequality gives
|c(C, Ao )| ≤ 6K0 e−κn , and the success identity gives the stated advantage bound. Lemma 3 includes
mixed product initialization. Appendix A provides the explicit constants.

5.3    Attaining exponential-order correlation
The following construction shows that the exponential-in-n order in Theorem 1 is attainable. Write
Zo = |0ih0| − |1ih1| for computational-basis measurement on the output qubit.

Proposition 14. For every n ≥ 1, put r = dn/4e. There is a zero-ancilla circuit Cn with at most
three multiqubit layers and at most n − r + 1 multiqubit gates such that
                                                         (
                                                          1,             r = 1,
                                         c(Cn , Zo ) =
                                                          22−r ,         r ≥ 2.

Consequently, c(Cn , Zo ) = exp[−(log 2)n/4 + O(1)] as n → ∞.

Proof. Partition the inputs into r nonempty blocks of size at most four. In a block of size b, label
the wires q1 , . . . , qb and store its parity on qb using the following two-layer CNOT schedule; i → j
denotes control qi and target qj , and a dash means no gate:

                                    b   first layer second layer
                                    1        —           —
                                    2      1→2           —
                                    3      1→2         2→3
                                    4 1 → 2, 3 → 4     2→4

The schedules use disjoint supports within each layer and run in parallel across blocks. Each CNOT,
and the generalized Toffoli below, is one allowed multiqubit gate up to local Hadamards, by the
equivalence in Section 2. The two preprocessing layers use n − r gates in total and leave the block
parities z1 , . . . , zr on the representative wires. If r = 1, measuring the representative already gives
parity exactly.
   For r ≥ 2, apply a generalized Toffoli in the third layer with controls z1 , . . . , zr−1 and target zr .
Thus the total gate count is n − r + 1. The target becomes y = zr ⊕ j<r zj . Under uniform input,
                                                                            Q

the block parities are independent uniform bits and their parity equals the input parity. Thus,
before a possible output NOT,
                                                                                         
                                  P                          P
                                         xi +y                         zj        Y
                          Ex (−1)    i           = Ez (−1)       j<r      1−2           zj 
                                                                                  j<r

                                                 = −2(−1)r−1 2−(r−1) = (−1)r 22−r .



                                                         22
The term without the product has mean zero, and the product is nonzero only when all r − 1 controls
are one. An output NOT when r is odd makes the correlation positive; this one-qubit gate is free in
the model. Measuring the target proves the formula and the gate count. Finally, r = n/4 + O(1)
gives the stated exponential order.

   The construction matches the order of decay, without optimizing the exponential constant. It
concerns uniform-input correlation: for n ≥ 9 its correlation is less than one, so its deterministic
output is incorrect on some inputs and its worst-case success probability is zero.


6     The exact depth-four gate lower bound
The shared event estimate also constrains exact computation through a fourth layer. We first retain
one variable per source without increasing gate count, then use output determinism to obtain a
certificate whose complexity depends on the gate count rather than on physical width.

6.1   Parity-preserving first-layer cleanup
We use the parity-preserving quantum restriction of [12, Lemma 4.1]. Its preparation of the fixed
two-qubit states within the original first layer is also part of that proof. We give the parity-only
argument with explicit circuit and resource accounting. Here a restriction may fix a pair of input
wires to a superposition of computational-basis strings of the same parity; it is not necessarily an
ordinary classical bit restriction.

Lemma 15 (Parity-preserving cleanup). Let C be an exact n-input parity circuit in the model
of Section 2, on N physical wires, with n ≥ 1 and pure product initialization. There is a circuit
C 0 on the same wires, with dn/3e ≤ r ≤ n variable inputs forming a subset of the original input
wires, that computes r-bit parity or its complement exactly on the same designated output wire, with
the same observable Ao , and does not increase entangling depth or multiqubit-gate count. Each
first-layer component of C 0 contains at most one variable input. Components here are gate supports
and individual idle wires, including untouched input singletons. All N − r ancillary wires of C 0 are
initialized in a fixed pure product state. Their number may exceed the original N − n: it is physical
wire count, not ancillary wire count, that is preserved.

Proof. Fix the first multiqubit layer D1 , padding with an empty layer if the circuit has none. If D1
is empty, every input wire is an idle singleton; leave the circuit unchanged and take r = n, which
proves the lemma in that case. Assume henceforth that D1 is nonempty.

Exactness permits fixed-parity substitutions. Use the output eigenvectors |a± i from Section 2.
For the original product ancillary state |αi, exactness gives

                                  C(|xi ⊗ |αi) = |aχ(x) i ∗ o ⊗ |γx i.

Let I ⊆ [n] P
            be a set of retained input positions. For a string t indexed by any subset of [n], use
               t
χ(t) = (−1) j j , the sum running over the positions of t; in particular the empty string has parity
sign one. Suppose the other input positions are fixed to a unit vector Φ = t ct |ti supported on
                                                                                  P

strings with χ(t) = ς ∈ {±1}. All tensor factors are placed on their original physical wires. For
z ∈ {0, 1}I , let x(z, t) combine the retained bits z and fixed-position bits t, and set
                                              X

                                              t

                                                                                !

The parenthesized garbage vector has norm one because Cι is an isometry and the output factor is
a unit vector. In particular, interference among the garbage vectors cannot spoil the deterministic

not merely a bounded-error guarantee on computational-basis inputs.

                          (|θg ihθg |)(φg ⊗ ψ) = 0,        Gg (φg ⊗ ψ) = φg ⊗ ψ

for every vector ψ on the other wires in the gate. Thus fixing this pair to φg deactivates the entire
gate, while all other k − 2 input wires remain variable. The selected pairs are disjoint because the
original gate supports are disjoint.
    For a first-layer gate with exactly two input wires, fix one of them to |0i and retain the gate on
its original support; deactivating it would leave no variable input, whereas fixing one wire keeps one.
It then has only one variable input; the fixed wire becomes an ancilla. Leave gates with one or zero
input wires unchanged, and leave every idle input wire variable. In particular, an input-free gate
contributes nothing to the count of variable inputs.

and let De keep be the product of the first-layer reflections that were not deactivated. Their supports
are mutually disjoint and are disjoint from the prepared pairs. Let |Ωz i be the product input state

    The layer D  e keep C replaces each deactivated gate by one two-qubit gate on a subset of its
original support and retains all other gates. It is therefore one entangling layer, with no increase in
multiqubit-gate count. The local conjugations that implement its product reflections and CNOTs
can be merged into the adjacent local layers. The suffix Csuf uses the original later multiqubit layers,
so the full entangling depth does not increase. All physical wires, including the output wire even if
it was one of the fixed inputs, are retained.
    Each prepared pair is now an input-free first-layer component. All other wires of a deactivated
gate are singleton components; in particular its surviving variable inputs are distinct sources. The
undeactivated input-containing gates have at most one variable input each. Since Ωz uses only fixed
single-qubit ancillary states, initialization remains a pure product. This does not assert that the
ancillary state after the first layer is product.

Count the retained inputs. Partition the original wires into first-layer gate supports and idle

For every integer k ≥ 0, r(k) ≥ k/3; equality in the nontrivial k ≥ 3 case occurs at k = 3. Since the
component input counts sum to n, their retained counts sum to an integer r ≥ n/3, hence r ≥ dn/3e.
This also covers n = 1, 2 and arbitrary input-free or idle components.

6.2   Small-support observables after three layers
We convert a product of one-qubit test operators at the output of three layers into a linear
combination of product events after two layers. The expansion is algebraic; the cleaned first-layer
assumption is needed only when applying the event bounds.

Set t = |S| ≤ s. A third-layer gate disjoint from S conjugates identity and has no effect. If h3 gates
meet S, then h3 ≤ t, because the gate supports are pairwise disjoint. Supported qubits idle in this
layer remain as individual tensor factors.
Step 2: expansion of the affected reflections. For an affected gate g with support supp(g), write
Dg = I − 2Πg with Πg = q∈supp(g) πq , where each πq is a rank-one orthogonal projector. For the
                         N

                               B

respectively. Each factor has operator norm at most one by submultiplicativity. When q ∈ / S, these

absolute sum at most
                                       (1 + 2 + 2 + 4)h3 = 9h3 .

                  Y = Y< + iY= ,           Y< = (Y + Y ∗ )/2,               Y= = (Y − Y ∗ )/(2i).

                               2

where the Pa , Qb are rank-one orthogonal projectors. Repeated eigenvalues cause no difficulty:
choose an orthonormal basis of the eigenspace; zero coefficients may be discarded. Consequently Y
is a linear combination of such projectors with coefficient absolute sum at most four. This need not
be a convex combination, and the coefficients for iY= may be imaginary.
    Apply this decomposition at each of the original t sites in each expanded tensor. Tensoring the
decompositions multiplies their coefficient absolute sums, so
                                          X                   X

where every Eν is a physical-qubit product event: each factor is an identity or a rank-one orthogonal

identity event with coefficient one; the same estimates hold using empty-product conventions. No
first-layer hypothesis was used in this algebraic expansion.
                                                                                       (2)
Step 4: application of the two-layer event bounds. For qν (x) = Tr(ρx Eν ), absorb the final local
layer L2 of C (2) into Eν . This again preserves its physical-qubit product-event form. Grouping its
one-qubit factors within each nonempty source–second-layer port produces a positive contraction on
that port, exactly as required by Theorem 11.
    The first-layer assumption supplies r independent one-input sources. All input-free first-layer
components can be grouped into a density-operator resource tensor-independent of those sources
and independent of x; this follows from product initialization and first-layer disjointness. The
intermediate local layer L1 acts within these groups, so it preserves this separation. Thus every qν
satisfies |qbν ([r])| ≤ K0 e−ar . Finally, linearity of the uniform signed average gives
                                                              X

The triangle inequality and ν |cν | ≤ 36s prove the claim. If S is empty, the coefficient is in fact

zero because r ≥ 1 and hIix = 1.

6.3   The exact last-layer certificate
The following argument uses only the final layer and exact output determinism, not the depth
or internal structure of the prefix. We use the identity/active-sector decomposition from [12,
Section 2.3.1] to derive an explicit quantitative certificate on one- and two-qubit product observables.

Lemma 17 (Exact last-layer certificate). Let a circuit in the model of Section 2 compute parity
exactly on n ≥ 1 input bits. Suppose the final multiqubit layer contains a gate incident to the
output qubit o, with b ≥ 1 other wires. Regard those wires as its controls in the product-reflection



                                                         27
representation. Let ρx be the state at the output of the prefix preceding that layer, with any preceding
local gates included, and put

                    α(B) = 2−n
                                   X
                                            χ(x) Tr(ρx B),        χ(x) = (−1)x1 +···+xn .
                                 x∈{0,1}n

There is a fixed Hermitian product contraction B, independent of x and supported on at most two
physical prefix-output qubits, such that
                                                          1
                                              α(B) ≥          .
                                                       2b + 1
Here a product contraction means a tensor product of one-qubit contractions, with identity on every
unspecified wire. If no gate in the final multiqubit layer touches o, there is instead a one-qubit
Hermitian unitary B with α(B) = 1.
Proof. Step 1: isolate the output gate. Absorb the terminal local rotation on o into its measurement
observable Ao . Exactness and n ≥ 1 make Ao a Hermitian unitary, by Section 2. All other terminal
local gates act outside o and do not change its statistics. Within the final multiqubit layer, gate
supports are disjoint. Writing that layer as U G, where G is the gate incident to o, the other gates
U commute with both G and Ao . Hence

                                       (U G)∗ Ao (U G) = GAo G.

Thus removing U does not change the output expectation, even when ρx is entangled across their
supports.
   Label the control wires by 1, . . . , b, separately from the input indices. In the gate’s product
basis, write
                  b
                  O
            P =         Pj ,   Q = I − P,        Ro = Io − 2πo ,        G = Q ⊗ Io + P ⊗ Ro ,
                  j=1

where Pj and πo are one-qubit rank-one orthogonal projectors. This representation is valid with any
incident wire chosen as the output; no distinguished target of a Toffoli representation is needed.
Suppressing identity tensor factors, set AG = GAo G. For every input, y = χ(x) satisfies

                     Tr(ρx AG ) = y,        Hx := I − yAG ≥ 0,          Tr(ρx Hx ) = 0.

Indeed, AG is a Hermitian unitary and Tr ρx = 1.
Step 2: exactness on each inactive control sector. For Qj = I − Pj , extended by identity off control
j, we have Qj P = 0, Qj G = GQj = Qj , and [Qj , Ao ] = 0. Consequently Qj commutes with both
AG and Hx and Qj AG = Qj Ao . Since Qj is an orthogonal projector,

                                             0 ≤ Qj Hx ≤ Hx .

Indeed, block decomposition with respect to Qj writes Hx as the sum of the positive operators
Qj Hx Qj and (I −Qj )Hx (I −Qj ), which proves this order inequality. Positivity of ρx and Tr(ρx Hx ) =
0 now give
                           0 = Tr(ρx Qj Hx ) = Tr(ρx Qj ) − y Tr(ρx Ao Qj ).
No projection of the state is performed or normalized here. Averaging the identity yields

                                  qj := Ex Tr(ρx Qj ) = α(Ao Qj ) ≥ 0.

                                                     28
   The commuting control projectors satisfy the operator union bound
                                             b
                                             Y                  b
                                                                X
                                   Q=I−          (I − Qj ) ≤          Qj .
                                             j=1                j=1

To see this, simultaneously diagonalize the Qj ; each eigenvalue is 0 or 1, and the indicator that at
least one eigenvalue is 1 is at most the number of 1’s. It follows that
                                                            b
                                                            X
                                      q := Ex Tr(ρx Q) ≤          qj .
                                                            j=1

No statistical independence of the control outcomes is assumed.
Step 3: obtain the quantitative certificate. Put A0o = Ro Ao Ro , a one-qubit Hermitian unitary. The
orthogonal P, Q sectors give the exact identities

                          AG = QAo + P A0o ,        AG − A0o = Q(Ao − A0o ).

Because Ao − A0o is Hermitian of norm at most two and acts only on o, it commutes with Q.
Therefore
                  −2Q ≤ AG − A0o ≤ 2Q,    | Tr(ρx (AG − A0o ))| ≤ 2 Tr(ρx Q).
Since α(AG ) = Ex y 2 = 1, averaging with the parity sign gives

                                           |1 − α(A0o )| ≤ 2q.

All the coefficients here are real. Keeping their signs and using the bound on q, we obtain
                                                               b
                             1 ≤ α(A0o ) + 2q ≤ α(A0o ) + 2
                                                               X
                                                                     α(Ao Qj ).
                                                               j=1

In particular, the following absolute-value form will also be useful:
                                                         b
                                                         X
                                1 ≤ |α(Ro Ao Ro )| + 2         |α(Ao Qj )|.                      (20)
                                                         j=1

The right-hand side of the signed inequality is at most

                           (2b + 1) max{α(A0o ), α(Ao Q1 ), . . . , α(Ao Qb )}.

Thus at least one of these coefficients is at least 1/(2b + 1), with its positive sign as claimed. The
corresponding operator is either the one-qubit Hermitian unitary A0o or a product Ao Qj of one-qubit
Hermitian contractions on two distinct wires. All choices are fixed independently of the input.
    If the final multiqubit layer has no gate on o, the same conjugation argument removes all its
gates from the output expectation. Exactness then gives Tr(ρx Ao ) = χ(x) and hence α(Ao ) = 1.
This also covers an empty final layer; a circuit with no multiqubit layer can be padded with an
empty layer. The proof uses neither purity of ρx nor a cleaned first layer; its positivity argument
does require the pointwise exactness assumption.

    Only the no-gate case and the identity-sector argument of Steps 2–3 are used below; Lemma 18
replaces the 1/(2b + 1) certificate by a gate-count inequality.

                                                   29
6.4   Control cells and completion of the lower bound
The preceding certificate has a prefactor depending on the number of controls of the final gate.
We replace individual controls by blocks, called cells, determined by their first-layer source and
their second- and third-layer incidences. Each cell lies in a single two-layer port and meets at most
one third-layer gate. These two properties allow its entire control projector to be treated as one
rank-one operator, with a cost independent of the number of physical qubits in the cell.

Lemma 18 (Cell certificate). Consider an exact parity circuit in the model of Section 2, on
N ≥ r ≥ 1 qubits with r variable inputs and fixed pure product ancillas. Write it with four multiqubit
layers, allowing empty layers and arbitrary intervening and boundary one-qubit gates. Suppose
every first-layer component that contains a variable input, including an idle variable-input singleton,
contains exactly one such input; wires carrying fixed original inputs count as ancillas. Let m2 , m3 ≥ 0
be the numbers of multiqubit gates in layers two and three.
    There is a nonnegative integer Ncell , depending only on the circuit, such that

                 1 ≤ [36 + 2664Ncell ]K0 e−ar ,       Ncell ≤ (r + 1)(m2 + 1)(m3 + 1).              (21)

The constants are those of Theorem 11. If the fourth multiqubit layer does not touch the output, one
may take Ncell = 0.

Proof. Step 1: fix the circuit stages and the event bound. Write

                           C = L4 D4 L3 D3 C (2) ,        C (2) = L2 D2 L1 D1 L0 ,

where the Lj are products of one-qubit unitaries and the Dj are disjoint controlled-Z layers. Let
 (2)
ρx be the state after C (2) , and let ρx be the state after L3 D3 C (2) , immediately before D4 . Absorb
L4 into the final output measurement, denoting its one-qubit Hermitian unitary by Ao , and set

                      α(B) = Ex∈{0,1}r χ(x) Tr(ρx B),          χ(x) = (−1)x1 +···+xr ,

with a uniform average.
    Put β = K0 e−ar . Theorem 11 bounds the absolute full-parity coefficient of every admissible two-
layer port-product event by β. Product initialization and first-layer disjointness give r independent
one-input sources. Group all input-free first-layer components into one density-operator resource
independent of these sources. Define its ports after grouping, as required by the theorem.
    If D4 does not touch o, Lemma 17 gives α(Ao ) = 1, and Lemma 16 with s = 1 gives 1 ≤ 36β.
This proves the assertion with Ncell = 0. Henceforth let G be the gate of D4 incident to o. All other
gates in D4 cancel from its output expectation, as in Lemma 17. Let T be the set of control wires
of G, excluding o. Write
                             O
                       P =         Pq ,   Q = I − P,         G = Q ⊗ Io + P ⊗ Ro ,
                             q∈T

where Pq are one-qubit rank-one orthogonal projectors and Ro is the induced one-qubit reflection.
Step 2: partition the controls into cells. For 1 ≤ i ≤ r, let V1,i be the wire set of input source i, and
let V1,0 be the union of the input-free first-layer components; V1,0 may be empty. For ` = 2, 3, let
V`,j be the support of gate j in layer `, for 1 ≤ j ≤ m` , and let V`,0 be the set of wires idle in that
layer. Define the cells to be the nonempty sets

              cijk = T ∩ V1,i ∩ V2,j ∩ V3,k ,     0 ≤ i ≤ r,     0 ≤ j ≤ m2 ,        0 ≤ k ≤ m3 .

                                                     30
Each wire has exactly one source label and one gate-or-idle label in each layer, so these cells partition
T . Their number satisfies
                                  Ncell ≤ (r + 1)(m2 + 1)(m3 + 1).
For j > 0, the cell lies in the port V1,i ∩ V2,j . For j = 0, it lies in the single private idle port V1,i ∩ V2,0 .
The global idle label therefore does not merge different source ports. Likewise, the cell lies entirely
in one third-layer gate if k > 0, and is entirely idle if k = 0. The output is excluded from every cell,
even if it has the same three labels. Tensor-factor reorderings used below are not physical SWAP
gates.
Step 3: apply the exact identity-sector argument to cells. For a cell c, put
                                              O
                                       Pc =         Pq ,        Qc = Ic − Pc ,
                                              q∈c

with identity extensions off c. The cells partition the controls, so P = c Pc and Q ≤ c Qc . Put
                                                                                           Q                 P

AG = GAo G and Hx = I − χ(x)AG . Exactness gives Hx ≥ 0 and Tr(ρx Hx ) = 0. Each Qc commutes
with Ao and G, annihilates P , and satisfies Qc G = GQc = Qc . The argument of Step 2 in the proof
of Lemma 17, the block decomposition of Hx with respect to a commuting orthogonal projector,
therefore applies verbatim to Qc , regardless of the dimension of the cell. It gives

                                        α(Ao Qc ) = Ex Tr(ρx Qc ) ≥ 0.

Combining the operator union bound with the comparison GAo G − Ro Ao Ro = Q(Ao − Ro Ao Ro ),
exactly as in that lemma, yields
                                                                 X
                                    1 ≤ |α(Ro Ao Ro )| + 2             |α(Ao Qc )|.                              (22)
                                                                   c

This uses neither independence of the cells nor commutation of ρx with their projectors. It is a
reuse of the proof’s identity-sector argument, not an assertion that a cell is one physical qubit.
Step 4: pull back one whole-cell projector. We prove, for each fixed cell c,

                                              |α(Ao Pc )| ≤ 1296β.
                                                                                      N
Write L3,q for the one-qubit factor of L3 on wire q, and put L3,c =                      q∈c L3,q . Define

                                   Aeo = L∗3,o Ao L3,o ,         Pec = L∗3,c Pc L3,c .

Then L∗3 (Ao Pc )L3 = Aeo Pec , where Aeo is a one-qubit contraction and Pec is still a product of one-qubit
rank-one orthogonal projectors on c. Cyclicity of trace gives
                                                           h                      i
                                    Tr(ρx Ao Pc ) = Tr ρ(2)
                                                        x D3 (Ao Pc )D3 .
                                                              e e

The observable meets at most two gates in D3 : one at o and one containing c. These gates may
coincide, or either may be absent. All other third-layer gates conjugate identity.
    For an affected gate Dg = I − 2Πg , expand its conjugation as

                                 Dg BDg = B − 2Πg B − 2BΠg + 4Πg BΠg .

Keep the coefficients 1, −2, −2, 4 separate from the operator factors. If h3 ≤ 2 gates are affected,
their simultaneous expansion has coefficient absolute sum at most 9h3 ≤ 81. In each scalar-free

                                                           31
branch, the output factor is a one-qubit contraction. If c is in gate g, let Πc be the tensor product
of the trigger projectors of Πg on c. The cell factor is one of

                                 Pec ,          Πc Pec ,     Pec Πc ,           Πc Pec Πc .

Each has rank at most one and norm at most one, since Pec , a tensor product of one-qubit rank-one
orthogonal projectors, is a rank-one orthogonal projector on the cell register, and so is Πc . If c
is idle, its factor is just Pec . Every physical-qubit factor outside {o} ∪ c is identity or a rank-one
orthogonal projector. When the output and cell meet the same gate, the branch choices on them
are synchronized, but each branch still factors over the disjoint blocks {o}, c, and the remaining
physical wires.
    For completeness, let Y be a rank-at-most-one contraction on an arbitrary finite-dimensional
space. If Y = 0, omit the term. Otherwise write Y = uv ∗ and put

                             Y< = (Y + Y ∗ )/2,                  Y= = (Y − Y ∗ )/(2i).

Both are Hermitian contractions whose ranges are contained in span{u, v}. Hence each has at most
two nonzero eigenvalues, all of absolute value at most one. Their separate spectral decompositions
express Y = Y< + iY= as a linear combination of rank-one orthogonal projectors with coefficient
absolute sum at most four. Repeated eigenvalues admit an orthonormal eigenbasis; zero eigenvalues
contribute nothing. The coefficients need not be positive or real. The one-qubit output contraction
also admits coefficient mass at most four, by the decomposition in Lemma 16.
    Applying these decompositions separately on the output and cell blocks gives a finite, input-
independent expansion
                                           X                     X
                      D3 (Aeo Pec )D3 =           dν Eν ,              |dν | ≤ 81 · 4 · 4 = 1296.
                                            ν                     ν

A spectral projector on c may be entangled across its physical wires. Nevertheless, c lies in one
source–second-layer port. For that port V , its factor in Eν has the form Πν,c ⊗ Eν,V \c , where Πν,c is
the cell’s rank-one spectral projector and Eν,V \c is a product of positive qubit contractions. This
includes any output factor in the same port. The two factors act on disjoint registers, so their
tensor product is a positive contraction. Every other port contains only positive qubit factors.
Thus regrouping Eν by the ports gives a tensor product of positive contractions, even when the cell
projector is entangled. This also applies to ports on the grouped resource source.
    To apply the two-layer bound, let τx be the state immediately before D2 . Up to tensor-factor
order, the first-layer separation gives
                                                             r
                                                             O
                                                  τx = σ ⊗            ρi,xi ,
                                                              i=1

where σ is a fixed density operator and each source state ρi,xi includes the local layer L1 . Thus
 (2)
ρx = L2 D2 τx D2 L∗2 . Set Fν = L∗2 Eν L2 . Local conjugation preserves positivity and port factorization,
including any entangled cell projector, and

                                         Tr(ρ(2)
                                             x Eν ) = Tr(Fν D2 τx D2 ).

The event theorem applied to Fν therefore gives

                                           Ex χ(x) Tr(ρ(2)
                                                       x Eν ) ≤ β.

Linearity and the triangle inequality prove |α(Ao Pc )| ≤ 1296β. No physical-product-only event
bound has been substituted for the port-product bound in this step.
Step 5: sum the cell certificate. Lemma 16 with s = 1 gives

                                       |α(Ao )|, |α(Ro Ao Ro )| ≤ 36β.

Since α(Ao Qc ) = α(Ao ) − α(Ao Pc ),

                                  |α(Ao Qc )| ≤ (36 + 1296)β = 1332β.

Substitution into (22) yields

                            1 ≤ 36β + 2Ncell (1332β) = [36 + 2664Ncell ]β.

This proves (21).

Proof of Theorem 2. By Lemma 3, it suffices to use pure product initialization. Let C be an exact
n-input circuit as in the theorem, with M multiqubit gates. Apply Lemma 15, obtaining a product-
initialized circuit on the same physical wires with dn/3e ≤ r ≤ n variable inputs and at most M
multiqubit gates. If its task is the complement of parity, reverse the output labels, replacing Ao by
−Ao . This changes neither depth nor gate count. Pad with empty layers at the end if necessary
to obtain four designated multiqubit layers. The first-layer source condition is preserved, and the
second- and third-layer gate counts satisfy m2 , m3 ≤ M .
    The exponential cell certificate gives

           1 ≤ [36 + 2664(r + 1)(M + 1)2 ]K0 e−ar ≤ (M + 1)2 K0 [36 + 2664(r + 1)]e−ar .

The second inequality uses (M + 1)2 ≥ 1. All quantities are positive, so taking natural logarithms
yields                                                                 
