B    The bounded-differences inequality
We record both the tail and exponential-moment forms of the bounded-differences inequality [14].
The proof uses the centered bounded-variable estimate of Hoeffding [10] and is included to specify
the constants used in the network argument.

                                                        34
Lemma 20 (Bounded differences and exponential moments). Let m ≥ 0 be an integer, and let
X1 , . . . , Xm be independent random variables, where Xj takes values in a finite set Xj , every point
of which has positive probability. Let Λ : m   j=1 Xj → R satisfy |Λ(x) − Λ(x0 )| ≤ cj whenever x, x0
                                             Q
                                                      Pm
differ only in coordinate j, where cj ≥ 0. Put V = j=1 c2j . Write Λ also for the random variable
Λ(X1 , . . . , Xm ). Then, for every real t,
                                                               2
                                              Eet(Λ−EΛ) ≤ et V /8 .                                    (23)

If V > 0, then for every u > 0,
                                                                            !
                                                            2u2
                                      P[Λ − EΛ ≥ u] ≤ exp −                      .
                                                             V

If V = 0, then Λ is constant on the product support and this upper-tail probability is zero. These
statements include m = 0, when the product support is a singleton and V = 0.
Proof. First let Y be a centered finite random variable in an interval of length cY . Its log moment
generating function ψY (t) = log EetY satisfies ψY (0) = ψY0 (0) = 0. Differentiating the finite sum
gives ψY00 (t) = Vart (Y ), where the subscript denotes the probability distribution tilted by the
positive factor etY . Its support remains in the same interval. If ymid is the interval midpoint, then
Vart (Y ) ≤ Et (Y − ymid )2 ≤ c2Y /4. Integrating twice gives ψY (t) ≤ t2 c2Y /8 for t ≥ 0; applying this to
−Y gives the same bound for t < 0.
    Let Fj = σ(X1 , . . . , Xj ), with F0 trivial, and set Λj = E[Λ | Fj ]. Then Λ0 = EΛ and
Λm = Λ. Fix preceding values x<j = (x1 , . . . , xj−1 ) and put gj (z) = EX>j Λ(x<j , z, X>j ), where
X>j = (Xj+1 , . . . , Xm ); an empty tuple is allowed. Independence makes this the same future law
for every z, so

                    |gj (z) − gj (z 0 )| ≤ EX>j |Λ(x<j , z, X>j ) − Λ(x<j , z 0 , X>j )| ≤ cj .

On this conditioning event, Λj = gj (Xj ) and Λj−1 = EXj gj (Xj ) is fixed. Thus Yj = Λj − Λj−1 has
conditional mean zero and lies in an interval of length at most cj . The centered-variable estimate,
applied separately to each conditional law, gives for every real t
                                                                   2 2
                                            E[etYj | Fj−1 ] ≤ et cj /8 .
           Pj
For Sj =    k=1 Yk , Sj−1 is Fj−1 -measurable. The tower property therefore gives
                                                                           2 2
                                        h                          i
                            EetSj = E etSj−1 E(etYj | Fj−1 ) ≤ et cj /8 EetSj−1 .

Iterating from S0 = 0 and using Sm = Λ − EΛ proves (23). For V > 0, exponential Markov gives
P[Λ − EΛ ≥ u] ≤ exp(−tu + t2 V /8) for t > 0; choose t = 4u/V . If V = 0, all coordinate oscillations
vanish. Any two points of the product support can be joined by successive single-coordinate changes,
so Λ is constant there. The empty product case has the same conclusion directly.

    Use of AI: The author prepared an eight-page draft without AI assistance, outlining previous
QAC lower bounds and several high-level strategies to extend them for the exact and bounded-error
parity QAC lower bounds at several depths. The author then fed this draft to multiple AI tools
(Claude, ChatGPT and two open-weight models with open-source harnesses) and prompted them to
work out the details of the proofs and identify missing gaps. The author fixed those missing gaps
and iteratively verified and expanded the proofs using AI tools. The author is solely responsible for
the correctness of the proofs.
